summary: Cape Breton light marking Little Bras d'Or: first lit 1874 a mile south on High Cape, moved to the point; fibreglass tower burned 2014, skeletal tower active.

structures.note: High Cape tower, a mile south of the point; in service to at least 1939 and gone by 1947 (LighthouseFriends)
Early 1960s skeletal tower on the point, 34 ft tall (LighthouseFriends); replaced 1989
Round white fibreglass tower; burned 21-23 February 2014 (LighthouseFriends; Rowlett)
Square skeletal tower carrying the active light (Rowlett; CCG list)

access.note: Canadian Coast Guard property. Point Aconi Road, 10.2 km (6.4 miles) from Highway 105; grounds open, tower closed (LighthouseFriends; Rowlett).

events.note: Put in operation 20 November 1874 on High Cape, a mile south of the point (LighthouseFriends)
Chief engineer recommends moving the light out to the extremity of the point; LighthouseFriends says this was not carried out for many years
Automatic whistling buoy placed in place of the can buoy previously maintained at Point Aconi, 1 July 1902
Fourth-order Fresnel lens installed in the lantern room (LighthouseFriends; not confirmed in a Department report read)
From fixed red to an occulting white, ten seconds on and five off (LighthouseFriends)
High Cape light gone by 1947 (LighthouseFriends); the photo essay gives 1943 to 1955 for its discontinuance (conflict)
Early 1960s: light established on the point itself on a skeletal tower; exact year not given (LighthouseFriends)
Round white fibreglass tower, 11.5 m (38 ft), replaces the skeletal tower (LighthouseFriends; Rowlett)
Station de-staffed in 1990, after the service of Carl D. Goyetche (LighthouseFriends)
Thieves broke in and stole copper wiring; light temporarily out of service (Rowlett)
Active light moved to a square skeletal tower, 10 m (33 ft) (Rowlett; CCG list gives square skeleton tower)
Fibreglass tower and nearby building burned to the ground, 21-23 February 2014; Rowlett calls the fire one of suspicious origin

resolved_conflicts.explanation: OpenStreetMap maps a standing structure, and LighthouseFriends and Rowlett say the 1989 fibreglass tower burned in February 2014. Both can be right about different towers: the 2012 square skeletal tower that carries the active light (listed by the Coast Guard as a square skeleton tower) still stands.

Rowlett gives a focal plane of 25.5 m (84 ft) and a white light of 2 s on, 4 s off for the 2012 light. The Coast Guard list gives a 26.9 m focal height and LFl W 6s, with the remark 'Flash 2 s; eclipse 4 s', which matches Rowlett's timing. The story gives the Coast Guard figures and notes Rowlett's focal plane.

notes_for_editor: Fact-check 2026-10-28: the 1901 list (p. 149, scan 260) and the 1907 keeper table (p. 143, scan 150) were checked on the Internet Archive page images; the appointment dates (18 April 1874; 6 November 1903) were read from those images because the OCR keeps the columns apart. The 1901 report's 'Since Little Bras d'Or...' passage is confirmed at p. 32 (scan 47); the Department's 1902 buoy entry at p. 78 (scan 91). The vmfaubert photo essay's 'built here in 1874' conflicts with LighthouseFriends and the 1901 report (High Cape); it is used in a footnote only. 1) Keepers: LighthouseFriends gives George Bonner 1874 to 1899, but the Department's 1901 report keeper list (scan 260) still names a George Bonner at Point Aconi. The story gives both and does not link him to John Charles Bonner. The 1907 keeper row (scan 150, p. 143) puts 'Bonner, John Charles Point Aconii' and 'Amero, Geo. D Pubnico' on one OCR line. The Bonner row is matched by column position. The 1910 Department table (volume 1911v45i13p21_0744) prints a '1903' date beside Bonner's name; I did not use it. 2) The LighthouseFriends quotation of the 1874 report is printed as the Annual Report 'for 1864'; that is evidently a typo, since LighthouseFriends dates the light to 1874 and to 'a decade later' than Ciboux Island (1864). The pre-1900 Canadian reports are not in the corpus, so 1874 rests on LighthouseFriends. 3) The photo essay (vmfaubert) places the first light at the point and gives 1943 to 1955 and 1955 to 1968 for the change; LighthouseFriends and the 1901 report do not support that placement. Used in a footnote only. 4) The 1915 lens and the change to an occulting white come only from LighthouseFriends. The 1916 Department works table lists Point Aconi among stations, but its columns do not line up with the names reliably, so I did not attribute the lens to it. 5) Chronicling America: two searches for Point Aconi gave no wreck or rescue at the station (one 1888 Richmond Dispatch hit is about the Fisheries Treaty and was not used). No storm, wreck or rescue tied to the station was found in the Department reports in the corpus, so the Storms chapter is omitted. 6) The record's characteristic (LFl W 6s), focal height (26.9 m) and range (14 nm) match the Coast Guard list (verified). The current tower in the record is the 2012 skeletal tower, not the burned 1989 fibreglass tower. 7) The 2011 theft and 2014 fire date come from Rowlett and LighthouseFriends respectively; both are secondary.
